name: Wolfgang Behringer
specialization: Global comparative witch-hunting; climate stress as contributing factor; comprehensive regional data synthesis

major_works.title: Witches and Witch-Hunts: A Global History
major_works.significance: Most comprehensive recent global comparative survey; introduced climate and social stress as systematic factors; provided comprehensive regional prosecution data

major_works.title: Hexen und Hexenprozesse in Deutschland (Witches and Witch Trials in Germany)
major_works.significance: Foundational German-language synthesis of German regional prosecution data; documents sources for German witchcraft studies

major_works.title: Shaman of Oberstdorf: Chonrad Stoeckhlin and the Phantoms of the Night
major_works.significance: Microhistorical case study of a German herdsman executed for witchcraft; engages with Ginzburg's night-journey traditions

core_argument: Witch-hunting was a global phenomenon with regional variations best understood through comparative analysis incorporating climate and social stress as contributing factors. The Little Ice Age (c.1560-1660) created crop failures, famines, and social anxiety that intensified demand for scapegoating and supernatural explanations; this environmental stress correlates with prosecution peaks across European regions.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Regional prosecution records across Europe and globally; climate data; comparative social and economic history
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Global distribution of witch prosecution; correlation of prosecution peaks with climate and social stress; comparative regional patterns
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Quantitative comparative analysis; climate history correlation; synthesis of regional studies
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Multi-causal macro-structural: environmental, social, and institutional factors interacting globally

key_contributions.claim: Prosecution peaks in Europe correlate significantly with periods of Little Ice Age cold, crop failure, and social stress; weather catastrophes created demand for witch-scapegoating
key_contributions.implication: Environmental history must be integrated into witch-hunting explanations

key_contributions.claim: Witch-hunting is not uniquely European; comparable phenomena occurred in Africa, Asia, and the Americas, often under different names and cultural frameworks
key_contributions.implication: European witch-hunting must be de-centered from a universal human narrative about scapegoating under stress

key_contributions.claim: Systematic compilation of regional prosecution statistics enables global comparison impossible from individual case studies
key_contributions.implication: Database methodology and synthesis work are essential for global-scale analysis

reception_and_critique.major_influences: German regional witchcraft history; climate history (Hubert Lamb); comparative global history methods
criticisms: Climate correlation thesis contested: some high-prosecution periods do not correlate with cold periods
Global comparisons risk flattening significant differences between culturally distinct phenomena
The micro-macro tension: his microhistory of Stoeckhlin demonstrates complexity that his global synthesis may obscure

historiographical_significance: Behringer produced the most comprehensive recent comparative synthesis of global witch-hunting and introduced climate history as a systematic analytical variable. His work bridges German regional expertise and global comparative ambition, making him central to current multi-causal approaches. His comprehensive German prosecution data remains a standard reference for Central European studies.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
